activities.anchor: a chain shift that happened once, in the ancestor of Germanic
activities.caption: pair each cognate set with its correspondence
activities.name: hlGrimmMatch

config.prompt: Grimm's law in the wild — pair each cognate set with its correspondence:

pairs.left: Latin cornu, canis / English horn, hound

pairs.right: descent, not borrowing — one sound, one rule

config.why: Because the shift ran over the whole inventory — every word, no exceptions — the correspondences are evidence of common descent, not resemblance.

activities.anchor: But there was a famous hitch
activities.caption: find the line that misreads the exception
activities.name: hlVernerSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary misreads Verner — click it:
lines: In 1877 Karl Verner showed the "exception" was another law.
The resulting fricatives voiced when the PIE accent fell on a later syllable.
PIE pətḗr (accent after the t) gave Germanic fadēr.
bhrā́ter (accent before the t) kept þ.
The Neogrammarian hypothesis: sound change keeps charming exceptions that need no explanation.
config.correction: Sound change is exceptionless within its environment — apparent exceptions dissolve into other laws, analogy, or borrowing.
config.why: One paradox became two regular laws — the discipline's founding demonstration, though some changes later proved to spread word by word (lexical diffusion, Labov).

activities.anchor: The comparative method is an engine for turning correspondences into a proto-language
activities.caption: line up the recipe that rebuilds dead languages
activities.name: hlRecipeOrder

config.prompt: The recipe — drag it into working order:
items: assemble cognate sets — descendants of one ancestor, not borrowings
tabulate the patterns across the sets
reconstruct the ancestral sound that best explains them
argue directionality from markedness and internal evidence
test the prediction — Hittite preserved Saussure's laryngeals as ḫ, exactly where predicted (Kuryłowicz, 1927)
config.why: A dead language partly verified by a prediction: no other human science reconstructs its unobservable past with this precision — Sanskrit pitar-, Greek patḗr, Latin pater, Gothic fadar give the p : p : p : f pattern and a proto-consonant *p.

activities.anchor: whose reconstructed tree matches the archaeology of a spread from Taiwan to Madagascar
activities.caption: call the Indo-European first-language share
activities.name: hlShareEstimate

config.prompt: What share of the world's people have Indo-European as their first language?
config.why: Roughly 46 per cent — and the reconstructed vocabulary reveals a pastoral, patriarchal, horse-and-wheel people, plausibly the steppe communities dated around 4500–2500 BCE, independently corroborated by ancient-DNA studies of Yamnaya remains (Haak and colleagues, 2015).
config.context: Austronesian's tree matches the widest pre-modern dispersal known — out to Easter Island.

activities.anchor: similar-sounding words for similar things prove that two languages are related
activities.caption: bet on what the nursery word proves
activities.name: hlMamaPredict

config.q: A word like "mama" turns up in unrelated languages worldwide. What does that prove?
choices: A single mother tongue for all humanity
Nothing about prehistory — chance resemblance; the word is a fact about babies' mouths
config.why: With a few thousand sounds available, unrelated languages collide constantly — which is why the comparative method insists on systematic correspondences across dozens of core vocabulary items, not isolated look-alikes.

activities.anchor: The family-tree model (Schleicher, 1860s) captures descent by splitting
activities.caption: drag the divider — the tree and the wave
activities.name: hlTreeCompare

config.prompt: Two models, needed jointly — drag the divider:

before.label: The tree (Schleicher, 1860s)
before.text: How languages branch apart over time — descent by splitting.

after.label: The wave (Schmidt)
after.text: Johannes Schmidt's alternative: innovations rolling geographically across dialect continua — real history needs both at once.

config.why: The method's reach: roughly 8,000–10,000 years before signals blur — beyond that, Nostratic and Altaic remain unproven and mass comparison lacks regularity. The dating fight: Gray and Atkinson's 2003 Bayesian date (~8,000–9,500 years, Anatolian farming) against the steppe hypothesis's archaeology and ancient DNA (~5,500 years).

activities.anchor: Two further disciplines complete the picture
activities.caption: true or false — running the columns with discipline
activities.name: hlSystemJudge

statements.s: Chain shifts keep the system balanced — when p emptied into f, b slid into the vacated p slot.
statements.why: A push chain: why the shift looks "designed".

statements.s: Latin spuere / English spit keeps p after s because fricatives did not shift after fricatives.
statements.why: The environment conditions the shift — regularity again.

statements.s: pedal keeps its p because the word was inherited through Germanic.
statements.why: It arrived by borrowing from Latin long after the shift — the method separates inherited words from learned ones, which is why English has both fatherly and paternal for one root.

statements.s: g → k shows in Greek genos against English kin.
statements.why: The voiced-stop column — rarer in attested material, since few classical languages kept plain *b.

activities.anchor: Borrowing is stratified by prestige and domain
activities.caption: adjudicate the evidence for descent
activities.name: hlContactBranch

config.root: Two languages share dozens of words for trade goods, plus a few look-alike nursery words. A colleague claims common descent. You have the methodological caution.

start.text: What can the shared vocabulary actually settle?

choices.label: Common descent — the vocabulary match settles it
choices.feedback: No: vocabulary moves with trade, prestige and conquest — shared nouns may record nothing but contact.

choices.label: Look for regular sound correspondences in core vocabulary and shared irregular morphology
choices.feedback: The strongest evidence of all: nobody borrows a paradigm like good/better/best.

choices.label: A sprachbund — neighbours converging without ancestry
choices.feedback: Possible if they are adjacent: the Balkan languages share a future construction no common ancestor explains — but the test is still correspondence.

contact.text: Shared vocabulary proves contact; only correspondences prove descent.

choices.label: So what would settle it?
choices.feedback: Regular sound correspondences in core vocabulary — and inherited irregularity.

descent.text: Family trees are drawn in inherited irregularity — and the Norse/English pair skirt and shirt shows how the same word can arrive twice.

area.text: Areal convergence is real — but so is the test: only regular correspondences in core vocabulary distinguish ancestry from neighbourhood.

choices.label: And the extreme case?
choices.feedback: Michif: Cree verb morphology with French noun phrases — two grammars fused by choice, not a creole.

config.why: Substratum effects, sprachbünde and mixed languages all blur the tree — which is exactly why the method demands regularity before it claims kinship.
